title: These are the words
hookLine: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell speech, retelling forty years
tomorrow: Devarim: the man of few words speaks

cards: Near the end of a life, some people want to tell their story. Not the whole thing, start to finish, but the parts that mattered, told their way, to the people who'll go on without them.
Grandparents do it at the kitchen table. Teachers do it in a last lecture. The fifth book of the Torah is that kind of telling.
Tradition says Moses has only weeks left. The people are camped across from the land he will never enter. And he begins to talk.

teach.h: ELEH HA-DEVARIM: THESE ARE THE WORDS.
teach.b: The book opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the words which Moses spoke unto all Israel beyond the Jordan." In Hebrew, Eleh ha-devarim. These are the words.
And that gives the book its Hebrew name: Devarim, words.
The English name, Deuteronomy, comes from the old Greek translation and means something like second law, from a phrase inside the book about a copy of the teaching.
The rabbis sometimes called it Mishneh Torah, the repetition of the Torah. Both names catch something.
Much of what Moses says, you've heard before: the Ten Commandments, the spies, the golden calf, laws about festivals and justice. But this time it's not the narrator telling it.
It's Moses, mostly speaking in his own voice, to a generation that was too young to remember, or wasn't born yet. And memory isn't a recording.
When Moses retells the spies, for example, he says it was the people who first asked to send them, a detail that isn't in the version in Numbers.

teach.h: THE STORY AS MOSES LIVED IT.
teach.b: This is the story as he lived it, and wants them to keep it. The book opens on the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year. By the end of it, Moses has died.
Jewish tradition counts the time between as only a few weeks.
So the whole book is a farewell: one long last conversation. A new part of the path begins here, portion by portion through Moses' last words. Before anything else, notice the frame.
The final thing the Torah gives is a person speaking to the people he loves.

how: Deuteronomy is read in synagogue from midsummer to early fall, ending on Simchat Torah, and its first portion, Devarim, is read on the Sabbath before Tisha B'Av, or on the day itself when Tisha B'Av falls on the Sabbath and the fast is postponed.

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.

s: Deuteronomy is told mostly by a narrator, like the earlier books
it's mostly Moses speaking in his own voice.
Moses' retelling of the spies adds that the people asked to send them
that detail is in Deuteronomy, not in the Numbers account.
Deuteronomy covers many years of Moses' life
it opens in the eleventh month of the fortieth year and ends with his death; tradition counts a few weeks.

games.q: you're Moses. you have a few weeks left, and the people at the river were children or unborn when it all began. what do you do?
o: write them a new code of law and leave.
tell them the whole story again, in your own words.
spend your last weeks alone on the mountain.
games.why: he tells it again: the journey, the laws, the mistakes, as he lived them. that's the book of Devarim.

practice: Think of something you're leaving behind, or already have: a home, a job, a season of life, someone who has died, a younger version of yourself.
Compose three or four lines of farewell to it, on paper or in your mind: what it gave you, what you want to remember. Let them be simple and true.

wordCard.voice: Devarim. Words. The Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, the book of Moses' farewell, from its opening line: these are the words.

orig.note: Hebrew: words, things; the Hebrew name of Deuteronomy, from its first verse.

carryVoice: Your line: last words matter. The whole book is one long, loving goodbye. Until tomorrow.
